questions.q: According to the curriculum, wellness is best described as…
options: A fixed state you reach and then maintain
The ongoing process of making choices across multiple dimensions of life
The same thing as being disease-free
questions.explain: Wellness is framed as an active, ongoing process — not a finish line.

questions.q: How many dimensions of wellness does the curriculum define?
questions.explain: Physical, emotional, intellectual, social, spiritual, occupational, environmental, and financial.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about weakness in one wellness dimension?
options: It stays isolated and doesn't affect others
It tends to spill into other dimensions
It only matters for physical health
questions.explain: The dimensions interact — strain in one area commonly shows up in others.

questions.q: What's the key difference between healthcare and wellness, per the curriculum?
options: Healthcare treats what's already gone wrong; wellness shapes how often that happens
Wellness replaces the need for healthcare
questions.explain: Healthcare is largely reactive; wellness is the daily-behavior layer that shapes risk beforehand.

questions.q: On the wellness spectrum described in the curriculum, what does “no diagnosis” represent?
questions.explain: Absence of disease sits in the middle of the spectrum — not at either end.

questions.q: According to the curriculum, what's true about detox products?
options: They outperform your liver and kidneys
They don't out-perform your liver and kidneys' normal function
They replace the need for sleep
questions.explain: Your liver and kidneys already do this job continuously — no product beats that baseline.

questions.q: Which is considered stronger evidence per the curriculum's guide to reading research?
questions.explain: Meta-analyses and RCTs sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy the curriculum describes.

questions.q: What does the curriculum recommend before changing any habits?
options: Observe your current patterns for a week first
Skip straight to the final module
questions.explain: A short observation period gives you an honest baseline before you start changing anything.

questions.q: How many calories per gram does fat provide, compared to protein or carbs (4 cal/g each)?
questions.explain: Fat is the most calorie-dense macronutrient at roughly 9 calories per gram.

questions.q: What's the curriculum's default guidance on supplementing micronutrients?
options: Everyone should supplement broadly as a default
Supplement for identified gaps, not as a blanket default
questions.explain: Supplementation is framed as gap-filling, not a default layer on top of a normal diet.

questions.q: Per the curriculum, what accounts for the majority of daily calories burned for most people?
questions.explain: Basal metabolic rate — the energy your body burns just staying alive — is the largest share for most people.

questions.q: What should you check first when reading a nutrition label?
options: Serving size and servings per package
questions.explain: Every other number on the label is relative to the stated serving size.

questions.q: Which category of processed food does the curriculum say is actually worth limiting?
options: Minimally processed foods like frozen vegetables
Ultra-processed food engineered for palatability and overconsumption
questions.explain: The concern is specifically ultra-processed food, not the broad, loosely-defined category of “processed.”

questions.q: The RDA of 0.8g/kg protein is described in the curriculum as…
options: The amount needed to prevent deficiency, not necessarily optimal for active adults
questions.explain: It's a deficiency-prevention floor, not a performance or active-lifestyle target.

questions.q: What does pairing carbs with protein or fat do, per the curriculum?
options: Blunts the blood sugar spike regardless of the carb's glycemic index
questions.explain: Pairing macronutrients slows digestion and blunts the resulting blood sugar spike.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about trans fat?
options: It has an established safe intake level
It has no established safe intake and should be avoided
It's the same as saturated fat
questions.explain: Unlike other fats, trans fat has no known safe intake threshold.

questions.q: What's described as a more responsive everyday hydration signal than fixed water targets?
questions.explain: Urine color gives real-time feedback that a fixed “8 glasses a day” rule can't.

questions.q: According to the curriculum, what's intermittent fasting's main benefit?
options: A unique metabolic effect no other diet has
Behavioral simplicity, not a unique metabolic effect
questions.explain: Its main advantage is that the eating-window rule is simple to follow, not a special metabolic edge.

questions.q: Per the curriculum, physical inactivity is…
options: Only a concern for older adults
An independent chronic disease risk factor
questions.explain: Inactivity itself is treated as a standalone risk factor, separate from diet or weight.

questions.q: What's described as one of the strongest predictors of long-term mortality risk in the research cited?
questions.explain: Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max) shows up repeatedly as one of the strongest predictors.

questions.q: Without strength training, age-related muscle loss can begin as early as…
questions.explain: Sarcopenia can begin surprisingly early — into your 30s — without resistance training.

questions.q: What's the difference between flexibility and mobility, per the curriculum?
options: Flexibility is passive range of motion; mobility is controlled, usable range of motion
questions.explain: Flexibility is passive stretch range; mobility is that range under active control.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say is required for continued strength adaptation?
questions.explain: Progressive overload — gradually increasing demand — is what keeps driving adaptation.

questions.q: Zone 2 training is roughly defined as…
options: 60-70% of max heart rate, a conversational pace
questions.explain: Zone 2 is an easy, conversational-pace effort — not a high-intensity zone.

questions.q: How many weekly sessions mixing strength and cardio does the curriculum say covers most general health goals?
questions.explain: A realistic 2-4 sessions a week is framed as sufficient for most general health goals.

questions.q: According to the curriculum, is soreness (DOMS) a reliable signal of workout effectiveness?
options: Yes — more soreness always means a better workout
No — it reflects normal repair, not workout quality
questions.explain: Soreness reflects the muscle-repair process, not a scorecard for how effective a session was.

questions.q: What drives most injuries, per the curriculum, more than the activity itself?
questions.explain: Ramping volume up too quickly is a bigger driver of injury than the activity chosen.

questions.q: How often does the curriculum suggest breaking up long sitting for desk workers?
options: Never, as long as you exercise once daily
questions.explain: Regular short breaks — roughly every 30-60 minutes — are recommended regardless of daily exercise.

questions.q: Sleep is described in the curriculum as…
options: A passive shutdown of the body
Active maintenance — waste clearance, memory consolidation, hormone regulation, immune repair
questions.explain: Sleep is framed as active maintenance work across multiple body systems, not a passive pause.

questions.q: Cutting sleep short disproportionately removes which stage?
questions.explain: REM sleep, concentrated later in the night, is disproportionately lost when sleep is cut short.

questions.q: What mainly regulates the circadian rhythm?
questions.explain: Light exposure is the primary driver that keeps the circadian clock synced.

questions.q: What matters more than most single environmental tweaks, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: A consistent sleep/wake schedule outweighs most one-off environmental adjustments.

questions.q: Why can afternoon coffee disrupt nighttime sleep?
options: Caffeine's roughly 5-6 hour half-life keeps it active into the night
Coffee only affects sleep if consumed after 9pm
questions.explain: Caffeine's long half-life means a meaningful dose is still active many hours later.

questions.q: What's the ideal nap length for boosting alertness without grogginess, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: A short 10-20 minute nap avoids dropping into deep sleep and the grogginess that follows.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say sleep trackers are best used for?
options: Coarse trends over time, not nightly precision
questions.explain: Trackers are useful for spotting broad trends, not as precise nightly measurement tools.

questions.q: What should you fix first when resetting a broken sleep schedule?
options: Wake time, anchored with morning light
questions.explain: Anchoring a consistent wake time with morning light is the recommended starting lever.

questions.q: The curriculum describes “languishing” as…
options: A common middle state — not ill, not thriving
questions.explain: Languishing sits between illness and thriving — a common, often unnamed middle state.

questions.q: What's a key difference between stress and anxiety per the curriculum?
options: Stress responds to an identifiable demand and resolves when it passes; anxiety can persist without a clear trigger
questions.explain: Stress is tied to a specific demand; anxiety can linger without one clear cause.

questions.q: What reliably cues the parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) system, per the curriculum?
options: Slow breathing, nature exposure, and social connection
questions.explain: Slow breathing, nature, and connection are cited as reliable parasympathetic cues.

questions.q: What does “regulation” mean in the curriculum's framing of emotions?
options: Experiencing emotions without being overwhelmed by them
questions.explain: Regulation means feeling emotions fully without being overwhelmed — not suppressing them.

questions.q: How many weeks of regular mindfulness practice does the curriculum cite as showing measurable effects?
questions.explain: Roughly 8 weeks of consistent practice is the figure cited for measurable effects.

questions.q: What matters more for journaling's benefits, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Showing up consistently matters far more than how polished or long each entry is.

questions.q: What did the longest-running study of adult life find to be the strongest predictor of long-term wellbeing?
questions.explain: The quality of close relationships came out as the strongest predictor in that long-running study.

questions.q: Chronic loneliness carries health risks comparable to…
questions.explain: The curriculum places chronic loneliness's health risk in the same range as smoking or obesity.

questions.q: What correlates with worse mood more, per the curriculum?
options: Total screen time regardless of type
questions.explain: Passive scrolling tracks with worse mood more than active, connection-based screen use.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say therapy is commonly used for?
options: Everyday difficulty, not only crisis or severe diagnosis
Only after multiple failed attempts to cope alone
questions.explain: Therapy is framed as a tool for everyday difficulty, not something reserved only for crisis.

questions.q: The stress response evolved for…
questions.explain: The stress response is an ancient system built for short-term physical threats, not chronic modern stressors.

questions.q: Which type of stress carries the significant health costs per the curriculum?
questions.explain: It's sustained, chronic stress — not brief acute stress — that drives most of the health cost.

questions.q: What does a slow, extended exhale do, per the curriculum?
options: Activates the vagus nerve, shifting toward a parasympathetic state
questions.explain: A long exhale stimulates the vagus nerve, nudging the body toward calm.

questions.q: What does cognitive reframing target?
questions.explain: Reframing works on how an event is interpreted, not the event itself.

questions.q: How does the curriculum describe boundaries?
questions.explain: Boundaries are framed as proactive statements of what you have capacity for, not confrontation.

questions.q: What three components does burnout involve together, per the curriculum?
options: Exhaustion, cynicism/detachment, and reduced sense of efficacy
questions.explain: Burnout is defined by exhaustion, cynicism or detachment, and a reduced sense of efficacy together.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about passive rest like scrolling?
options: It's less restorative than genuinely engaging activities
questions.explain: Passive rest is less genuinely restorative than activities that actively engage you.

questions.q: What kind of plan is described as more usable in the moment than a general intention?
options: A specific, written “when X happens, I do Y” plan
A plan created during a crisis
questions.explain: A specific if-then plan is far easier to actually use in the moment than a vague intention.

questions.q: Why does screening matter, per the curriculum?
options: It catches conditions when treatment is simplest and most effective
It replaces the need for treatment
It's only useful after symptoms appear
questions.explain: Screening's value is catching conditions early, when treatment is simplest and works best.

questions.q: What improves how much gets covered in a short annual checkup appointment?
questions.explain: A written question list helps make the most of limited appointment time.

questions.q: What matters more than any single lipid panel snapshot, per the curriculum?
options: The exact date of the test
questions.explain: Trends across multiple tests over years matter more than any one snapshot value.

questions.q: Per current guidance cited in the curriculum, hypertension is commonly defined starting at…
questions.explain: 130/80 mmHg is the threshold cited from current AHA guidance.

questions.q: What can shift cancer screening timelines earlier, per the curriculum?
options: Family history, especially in a first-degree relative
questions.explain: A first-degree relative's history can move recommended screening ages earlier.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about adult vaccination needs?
options: Childhood vaccination covers everything needed for life
Several vaccines require adult boosters that childhood vaccination doesn't cover
questions.explain: A number of vaccines need adult boosters — childhood coverage alone isn't the full picture.

questions.q: What is gum disease linked to, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Gum disease is linked to broader systemic risks, including cardiovascular and diabetes risk.

questions.q: What does the curriculum call family history?
options: A free, powerful, and commonly underused preventive care tool
questions.explain: Family history is framed as a free, high-value tool most people underuse.

questions.q: Which is more valuable per the curriculum — a basic, regularly updated personal health record, or an elaborate unmaintained one?
options: A record kept only by your doctor
questions.explain: A simple record that's actually kept up to date beats an elaborate one that isn't.

questions.q: What's the four-part habit loop described in the curriculum?
questions.explain: Cue, craving, response, reward is the four-part loop the curriculum builds on.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about willpower?
options: It depletes across the day, so relying on it means relying on your weakest state
It's the most reliable behavior-change tool
It only affects diet, not other habits
questions.explain: Willpower is treated as a depleting resource — a fragile thing to build a whole strategy on.

questions.q: What does “habit stacking” attach a new behavior to?
questions.explain: Habit stacking anchors a new behavior right after one you already do automatically.

questions.q: What does the curriculum recommend for unwanted habits?
questions.explain: Deliberately adding friction makes an unwanted habit harder to fall into.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about a missed tracking day?
options: It's a failure that ends the habit
It means starting over from scratch
questions.explain: A missed day is treated as information to learn from, not a reason to quit.

questions.q: What guideline does the curriculum give for handling a lapse?
options: Wait a month before trying again
questions.explain: “Never miss twice” keeps one slip from turning into a longer break.

questions.q: What does the “1% better” framework emphasize?
options: Small daily improvements that compound over time
questions.explain: Small, compounding daily gains — not dramatic overhauls — are the framework's core idea.

questions.q: How many simultaneous new habits does the curriculum recommend as a reasonable ceiling?
options: None — one at a time only, ever
questions.explain: One to three at a time is the recommended ceiling for keeping change manageable.

questions.q: What's a normal menstrual cycle length range cited in the curriculum?
questions.explain: A normal cycle can range roughly 21-35 days — 28 is an average, not a fixed rule.

questions.q: What do reproductive hormones interact closely with, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Reproductive hormones interact closely with thyroid, cortisol, and insulin, not in isolation.

questions.q: The fertile window is roughly how many days around ovulation?
questions.explain: The fertile window spans roughly 6 days, not just the single day of ovulation.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say is often under-supported relative to pregnancy itself?
questions.explain: Postpartum recovery, especially mental health, is flagged as commonly under-supported.

questions.q: Menopause is clinically defined as…
questions.explain: Menopause is marked at 12 consecutive months without a period.

questions.q: Why does bone loss accelerate after menopause, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Declining estrogen after menopause is the driver of accelerated bone loss.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about mammograms and Pap/HPV testing?
options: They're well-established programs with strong mortality-reduction evidence
They replace the need for self-exams entirely
questions.explain: Both are described as well-established screening programs with strong evidence behind them.

questions.q: Which nutrient needs shift meaningfully across reproductive years, pregnancy, and menopause, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Iron, calcium, and folate needs shift notably across these life stages.

questions.q: What's required to diagnose low testosterone, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Diagnosis needs both blood testing and symptoms together, not either alone.

questions.q: How does the curriculum describe the PSA screening decision?
options: A universal default test for all men
A shared-decision conversation with a doctor
questions.explain: PSA screening is framed as a shared decision made with a doctor, not a blanket default.

questions.q: Men typically face cardiovascular risk how much earlier than women on average, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: On average, men's cardiovascular risk rises roughly a decade earlier than women's.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say about men and mental health support?
options: Men seek support at equal or higher rates than women
Men are less likely to seek support despite comparable rates of underlying struggle
Men rarely struggle with mental health
It's not addressed in the curriculum
questions.explain: Men seek support less often, even though underlying struggle rates are comparable.

questions.q: Male factors contribute to roughly what share of couples' fertility challenges, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Male factors are involved in roughly 40-50% of couples' fertility challenges.

questions.q: When does sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) accelerate, per the curriculum, without resistance training?
questions.explain: Without resistance training, meaningful muscle loss tends to accelerate from around age 40.

questions.q: What three areas round out core preventive priorities for men, per the curriculum?
options: Colorectal screening, prostate conversations, and mental health check-ins
questions.explain: These three areas are highlighted as core preventive priorities alongside cardiovascular health.

questions.q: What does the strongest longevity evidence support, per the curriculum?
options: Unglamorous fundamentals — exercise, sleep, diet, connection, not smoking
questions.explain: The strongest evidence backs consistent fundamentals, not novel or exotic interventions.

questions.q: What does “healthspan” measure?
options: Total years lived regardless of health
Years lived in good functional health
questions.explain: Healthspan tracks years lived in good functional health, distinct from raw lifespan.

questions.q: What's described as the most effective countermeasure to age-related muscle mass decline?
questions.explain: Strength training is the most effective tool against age-related muscle loss.

questions.q: What are the strongest evidence-backed fall-prevention tools, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Leg strength and balance training have the strongest evidence for preventing falls.

questions.q: What builds cognitive reserve more, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Genuinely novel learning builds cognitive reserve more than repeating familiar tasks.

questions.q: What's described as among the strongest predictors of all-cause mortality risk?
questions.explain: Cardiorespiratory fitness is again cited as one of the strongest predictors of mortality risk.

questions.q: The longevity effect size of strong social relationships is compared to…
questions.explain: Strong social ties carry a longevity effect comparable to quitting smoking.

questions.q: Which supplements does the curriculum say have reasonably solid evidence for specific gaps?
options: Vitamin D, omega-3s, creatine, and protein powder
questions.explain: These four are singled out as having reasonably solid evidence for filling specific gaps.

questions.q: What does the evidence actually support, per the curriculum's closing takeaway on longevity?
options: Consistency over decades, not a novel protocol
questions.explain: Decades of consistency — not a clever new protocol — is what the evidence actually supports.

questions.q: What matters more than a single “perfect” static posture, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Varying your posture and movement matters more than any single fixed “perfect” position.

questions.q: What does the 20-20-20 rule address?
questions.explain: The 20-20-20 rule is a simple technique for reducing digital eye strain.

questions.q: What does constant availability increase, per the curriculum, even without actual interruptions?
questions.explain: Just knowing you might be interrupted raises anticipatory stress, whether or not it happens.

questions.q: What outperforms optional wellness perks, per the curriculum?
options: Structural interventions like flexibility, usable PTO, and manageable workload
questions.explain: Structural changes to workload and flexibility outperform optional add-on perks.

questions.q: What does remote work remove that an office naturally provided, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: An office naturally supplies boundary and social cues that remote work removes by default.

questions.q: How does burnout research frame burnout, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Burnout is framed primarily as a mismatch in workplace design, not a personal failing.

questions.q: What does team wellness culture follow more, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: What leaders actually model day to day shapes culture more than the written policy does.

questions.q: What's generally more useful to track day-to-day, per the curriculum?
questions.explain: Process goals — the actions you control daily — are more useful to track than distant outcomes.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say time and energy are?
options: Both finite resources worth budgeting deliberately, and not the same thing
questions.explain: Time and energy are treated as two distinct finite resources, each worth budgeting on its own.

questions.q: How many dimensions does the wellness wheel self-assessment score?
questions.explain: It scores the same eight dimensions introduced back in Module 1.

questions.q: What's described as a reasonable ceiling for simultaneous new habits?
questions.explain: Consistent with the habit-formation module, three is the reasonable ceiling.

questions.q: What's the difference between leading and lagging indicators, per the curriculum?
options: Leading indicators are actionable daily process; lagging indicators confirm whether it's working
questions.explain: Leading indicators drive daily action; lagging indicators tell you later whether it worked.

questions.q: What does this curriculum say about its own role, per the final module?
options: It builds an informed baseline but doesn't replace individualized professional guidance
It's a substitute for a doctor
questions.explain: The curriculum positions itself as a knowledge baseline, explicitly not a replacement for professional care.

questions.q: How often does the curriculum recommend reviewing your wellness plan?
options: Never — set it and forget it
questions.explain: A quarterly review cadence is recommended to keep the plan realistic and current.

questions.q: What does the curriculum say a realistic first year looks like?
options: Building habits in months 1-3, reviewing and expanding in 4-6, layering in prevention in 7-12
questions.explain: A phased 12-month roadmap — not one big overhaul — is the realistic structure described.
